title: Why does my child add the wrong ending to a word?
meta_description: A child adds the wrong ending when a spelling rule is used without its condition. See how doubling, dropping the e and y to i work, and how to spot it.
hero_image_alt: A navy ribbon and a narrower gold ribbon joined end to end with a small knot on grey linen, beside a wooden spool and a wooden peg, in soft lamp light.
content_html:
Most of the rules in the national curriculum spelling appendix for adding an ending carry a condition: the first letter of the ending, the number of syllables, which syllable is stressed, or the letters the word ends in. A child who doubles a letter that should stay single, or keeps an e that should be dropped, has usually applied a rule where its condition does not hold.

Key takeaways

  • The final e of a root word is dropped before an ending that begins with a vowel letter. It survives before ment, ness, ful, less and ly, which are added straight on without changing the last letter.
  • Doubling depends on the number of syllables and, in longer words, on which syllable is stressed, so one rule does not cover every short vowel word.
  • The appendix gives two separate rules for y, one for adding es and one for adding ed, ing, er and est. Only the second mentions ing, and only the second requires a consonant letter before the y.
  • Which kind of error a child made usually points to the one question that was not asked, which is quicker than relearning every rule.
  • Once the rule is clear, the whole word still has to be written from memory, which is what look, cover, write, check does.

Why do children add the wrong ending to a word?

Children add the wrong ending when a rule has been learnt without its condition, or when the condition is hard to see in the word. That is reasoning from how the rules are worded, not a finding from a study of children’s errors: the appendix does not describe errors at all.

Take doubling. A short rule such as "double the last letter" sounds complete, while the appendix ties it to four things at once. A child who has the short version will be right often enough to trust it, and wrong exactly where the longer version matters.

The rules are also spread across year groups, so one a child half knows may be one they have not yet been taught in full. For the wider picture, see the earlier post on prefixes and suffixes.

When is the final e dropped, and when does it stay?

The appendix states the dropping as a rule and leaves the keeping to a different rule, though the two are often quoted as one.

The dropping rule, in Year 2, says the e at the end of the root word is dropped before ing, ed, er, est, y or any other suffix beginning with a vowel letter. Its examples are hiking, hiked, hiker, nicer, nicest and shiny, with being as an exception.

That row does not say the e is kept before anything. What the appendix says, in a separate Year 2 rule for the suffixes ment, ness, ful, less and ly, is that such a suffix is added straight on to most root words without any change to the last letter, which is why the e survives. Its examples include enjoyment, sadness, careful, hopeless and badly, with argument as an exception.

Two further rules keep the e before a vowel ending: the e after c or g is kept before able, or those letters would take their hard sounds, as in noticeable and changeable; and a final e is kept before ous where the soft g sound is needed, as in courageous.

A child who writes hopeing has treated a vowel ending as a consonant one, and a child who writes carful has done the reverse. Both come from the same unasked question: does the ending start with a vowel letter or a consonant letter?

When is a letter doubled?

A letter is doubled when the vowel before it needs to stay short and the ending begins with a vowel letter, but the conditions differ by word length. The four situations are spread across three year groups.

SituationWhat the appendix saysIts examples
One syllable word with a single consonant letter after a single vowel letter (Year 2)The last consonant letter of the root word is doubled, to keep the vowel short, before endings such as ing, ed, er, est and ypatting, humming, sadder, fatter
Verb or adjective ending in two consonant letters (Year 1)The ending is simply added onhunting, hunted, grander, fresher
Word of more than one syllable with the last syllable stressed (Years 3 and 4)The final consonant letter is doubled before any ending beginning with a vowel letterforgetting, preferred
Word of more than one syllable with the last syllable unstressed (Years 3 and 4)The consonant letter is not doubledgardening, limited

The appendix adds two limits. The letter x is never doubled: mixing, mixed, boxer, sixes. And for words ending in fer, in Years 5 and 6, the r is doubled only if the fer is still stressed once the ending is added, as in referring and preferred.

The stress rule is the hardest of these to apply, because it depends on hearing which syllable is stressed. Saying the word aloud and exaggerating the stress is one way to make it audible, though the appendix does not suggest it.

When does y change to i?

The appendix gives two separate rules for words ending in y, covering different endings. Quoting them as one rule is an easy way to go wrong, because the ing exclusion and the consonant condition belong to the second rule only.

The first, in Year 2, covers adding es to nouns and verbs ending in y: the y is changed to i before es is added. Its examples are flies, tries, replies, copies, babies and carries, and it says nothing about ing.

The second, also in Year 2, covers adding ed, ing, er and est to a root word ending in y with a consonant letter before it. Here the y changes to i before ed, er and est, but not before ing, because that would result in ii; the appendix notes that the only ordinary words with ii are skiing and taxiing. Its examples are copied, copier, happier, happiest, cried and replied, and then copying, crying and replying.

The ly ending has its own condition, stated in Year 2 and again in Years 3 and 4: where the root ends in y with a consonant letter before it, the y changes to i only if the root has more than one syllable, as in happily and angrily.

A child who writes copiing has applied the change to the ending it does not reach. A child who writes happyly has not applied it where it does. In both cases the question to ask is which ending is being added.

What does research say about how children learn suffixes in writing?

A 2011 study in the Journal of Child Language looked at ten beginning spellers with a mean age of five years and five months, coding the spellings in journals the children kept in kindergarten and grade one. Its abstract reports that the order in which the children learned to spell inflectional suffixes correctly is similar to the order in which they learn to use them in oral language before school age.

That is a narrow finding from a small group of very young children, and it is about the order in which suffixes are mastered rather than how to teach the rules. The page retrieved for this post names only one author in its metadata, so no authors are named below.

How can a parent tell which rule has gone wrong?

The quickest route is to sort the error into one of four types and ask the question that belongs to it. This is a way of using the rules above, not a method that has been tested.

What the child wroteQuestion to ask
A letter doubled that should not beHow many syllables does the word have, and is the last one stressed?
A letter not doubled that should beIs it a one syllable word with a single consonant after a single vowel letter?
An e kept or droppedDoes the ending begin with a vowel letter or a consonant letter?
A y kept or changedWhich ending is being added, and is there a consonant letter before the y?

Once the question is answered, practise the whole word: look at the corrected word, cover it, write it from memory and check it. The method is set out on the page about look, cover, write, check, and how spelling sticks explains how recall fits into learning a word.

A rule helps with the ending but does not replace learning the word. The appendix lists exceptions beside several of its rules, so a child who gets a word wrong despite knowing the rule may have met one of them.

Frequently asked questions

Is there one rule that covers all the endings?

No. Each ending has its own rule, condition and exceptions. Being is an exception to the drop the e rule, argument to the rule for adding ment, ness, ful and less, and truly, duly and wholly to the Years 3 and 4 rule for adding ly.

Why does the letter x never get doubled?

The appendix states that the letter x is never doubled and gives mixing, mixed, boxer and sixes as examples. It does not give a reason, so this post does not offer one.

Should a child learn the rules or just the words?

Both are useful and the appendix does not say which should come first. A child who has met the rule in class may find the weekly list easier, and a child who finds a list hard may be helped by seeing the rule behind its words.

Which year do children learn these endings?

Year 1 covers adding an ending to a verb or adjective ending in two consonant letters. Year 2 holds the one syllable doubling rule, the drop the e rule and both y rules. Years 3 and 4 add the stress based doubling rule and the rules for ly and ous, and Years 5 and 6 the rules for fer and able.

Can a child practise these endings without the whole list?

Yes. Look, cover, write, check works on any single word. Choose the misspelt word, work out which question was missed, and practise that word on its own.

Our FAQ page answers common questions about practising at home. If your child practises a weekly list, Spelling Nest keeps the same look, cover, write, check method alongside the writing.
